meta.title: Cross-validation done wrong and done right
meta.tools: k-fold, blocked and grouped cross-validation written from scratch, a 1-nearest-neighbour and an LDA classifier, leakage through overlapping windows and through shared subjects on real EMG, the 'feature selection outside the loop' trap on pure noise, nested cross-validation for a tuned hyper-parameter
meta.summary: Measure how much an accuracy estimate is inflated by four common validation mistakes — overlapping windows split at random, the same person in train and test, feature selection before splitting, and reporting the score used for tuning — using real EMG data and a pure-noise control.
meta.problem: The same classifier can be reported at 99 % or 80 % depending on how the data were split. Which number predicts performance on new data?
meta.theory:
Cross-validation estimates generalisation only if test samples are independent of everything used for fitting. (1) Windows that overlap by 50 % share raw samples with their neighbours; a random split puts near-copies of test windows in
the training set (fatal for nearest-neighbour methods). (2) Windows of one person are more alike than windows of different people: random splits measure within-person accuracy, not performance on a new user. (3) Any step that saw the labels —
including feature selection — must be inside the loop; selecting the 20 best of 5000 noise features on all data yields high 'accuracy' on noise. (4) The best cross-validated score over a grid of hyper-parameters is optimistically biased;
nesting the selection removes the bias. Expected honest result on noise: 50 %.
meta.method:
EMG gestures (32 features, 36 subjects, 2 recordings each). (1) Per subject, recording 1 only: random 5-fold vs 5 contiguous blocks per gesture vs train on recording 1 / test on recording 2, with 1-NN and LDA. (2) Pooled windows: random 6-fold vs
leave-6-subjects-out. (3) 60 samples × 5000 Gaussian noise features, random labels, 200 repetitions. (4) LDA shrinkage chosen from 8 values on 12 subjects' first 60 windows: best CV score vs nested CV vs a fresh test set.
meta.data: UCI 'EMG data for gestures' (Lobov et al. 2018).

rows.quantity: My expectation: 1-NN on randomly split overlapping windows looks near-perfect (> 98 %; 1 = yes)
Leakage through overlap: random split beats blocked split for 1-NN (1 = yes)
… and the blocked estimate in turn beats a separate recording session (1 = yes)
Pooled data: random 6-fold overestimates accuracy on people never seen (random > leave-subjects-out; 1 = yes)
Pure noise, feature selection inside the CV loop: accuracy = chance
Pure noise, features selected on all data first: 'accuracy' far above chance (> 85 %; 1 = yes)
Tuning bias: the best CV score over 8 shrinkage values exceeds the nested-CV estimate (1 = yes)
Nested CV is closer than the best tuning score to accuracy on fresh windows of the same recording (1 = yes)
